title: The Branch and the Cleansed City
summary: After the devastation of war, seven women beg one man to marry them so they will not bear the shame of being unmarried. Then the tone changes: on that day the Branch of the Lord will be beautiful and glorious, the survivors in Zion will be called holy, and the Lord will wash away Jerusalem's filth by a spirit of judgment and fire. Over the whole city he will create a cloud by day and fire by night, a canopy of glory and a shelter from heat and storm.
story: This short chapter completes the section that began in 2:1. That section opened with a vision of Zion exalted (2:2-4), then passed through judgment on pride (chapter 2) and the collapse of Jerusalem's society (chapter 3). Verse 1 finishes the picture of chapter 3, where the city's men fell in battle. Verses 2 to 6 answer the opening vision: after the purging, a holy remnant will live in a Jerusalem covered by God's presence as Israel once was in the wilderness. The pattern of chapters 2 to 4, hope then judgment then hope, is typical of Isaiah, who never lets either word stand alone. The Branch introduced here will grow into a major figure in the prophets.
historical:
Verse 1 assumes the aftermath of a war that killed so many men that women outnumbered them seven to one. Such a scene fits the Assyrian and Babylonian invasions that devastated Judah over the following century and a half. Verses 2 to 6 look beyond any specific date to the time after judgment, when a remnant remains in Jerusalem. On the traditional view Isaiah foresaw this in the eighth century BC; many critical scholars date the passage, with its vision of a purified remnant, to the period after the exile, when such hopes were especially alive. The book does not date the oracle itself.

The title Branch appears later in Jeremiah (23:5; 33:15) and Zechariah (3:8; 6:12), where it clearly names a coming king from David's line, and in Zechariah it is also linked with Joshua the high priest after the return from exile. Whether Isaiah 4:2 already carries that royal sense is debated, as the word note and the hard question below explain.
cultural:
In ancient Israel a woman without a husband had little economic security and often suffered social disgrace, especially if she had no children. Under normal custom a husband provided his wife's food and clothing (Exodus 21:10 lists food, clothing, and marital rights as a wife's due). The women of verse 1 offer to give up those rights and support themselves, asking only for his name, that is, the legal and social standing of marriage. The picture is of a society so emptied of men that ordinary protections have broken down.

The cloud by day and fire by night recall the pillar of cloud and fire that led Israel out of Egypt and through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21-22) and the cloud that filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-38). The canopy (Hebrew chuppah) was a covering or chamber, and in later Jewish custom the same word came to name the wedding canopy under which a couple is married, though that use is later than Isaiah. Book of life language, being recorded among the living (verse 3), reflects the practice of keeping registers of citizens; Moses speaks of God's book in Exodus 32:32.
literary: Verse 1 is prose-like in its bluntness and belongs with the end of chapter 3; the chapter division here is not ideal. Verses 2 to 6 are a single oracle of salvation, introduced by on that day, the same phrase that has introduced judgment in chapters 2 and 3. The same day of the Lord that humbles the proud will glorify the remnant. The oracle moves in three steps: the Branch and the fruit of the land (verse 2), the holy remnant (verses 3-4), and God's protecting presence (verses 5-6). The verb create in verse 5 is the verb of Genesis 1, suggesting that restored Zion is a new creation.

outline.t: The Branch of the Lord and the fruit of the land
A holy remnant, washed and cleansed
Cloud, fire, and canopy over Zion

doctrines.note: Those who remain in Zion will be called holy, not because they earned it but because the Lord has washed away their filth. Holiness here is God's gift through judgment and cleansing.
Judgment is not the end. The Lord promises beauty, glory, and protection for the survivors, and he promises to be present with them as in the exodus.

If the Branch of the Lord is a person, as later prophets use the term, verse 2 is the first glimpse in Isaiah of a coming royal figure. If it refers to the land's growth, it still anticipates the fruitfulness of God's renewed kingdom.

words.note: Tsemach, sprout or branch, something that springs up from the ground. In verse 2 it may mean the growth God gives the land, parallel to the fruit of the land, or it may be a title for a coming king. Jeremiah 23:5 and Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12 use the same word as a messianic title, and many interpreters, Jewish and Christian, read Isaiah 4:2 in that light.

Bara, to create, the verb of Genesis 1:1, used in the Hebrew Bible only with God as subject. In verse 5 the Lord creates a cloud and fire over Zion, marking the restored city as a new act of God, not a human achievement.

Chuppah, canopy or covering. Here it pictures God's glory spread over Jerusalem as a protecting shelter. The word is rare in the Old Testament; in Joel 2:16 and Psalm 19:5 it refers to a bridal chamber, and in later Jewish practice it became the name for the wedding canopy.

christ: Christians have read the Branch of verse 2 in light of the later prophets who clearly use it for the Davidic king, and so as pointing to Jesus. That link is honest but should be held carefully, since Isaiah 4:2 may speak of the land's fruitfulness; Isaiah 11:1 uses a different word for the shoot from Jesse, and it is there that the royal hope becomes unmistakable. More broadly, the chapter's promise of a people washed and made holy by a spirit of judgment and fire resonates with John the Baptist's announcement that the coming one would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (Matthew 3:11). The cloud of glory over God's people reaches its New Testament fulfillment in the Word who dwelt among us and whose glory was seen (John 1:14), and in the vision of a city whose light is the glory of God (Revelation 21:23).

hard.q: Is the Branch of the Lord in verse 2 the Messiah or simply the produce of the land?
hard.a: Both readings have strong defenders. Those who read it as a messianic title note that tsemach becomes a technical name for the coming king in Jeremiah and Zechariah, that the Aramaic Targum (an ancient Jewish paraphrase) renders the verse as the Messiah of the Lord, and that the pairing with the fruit of the land could describe the king and his people together. Those who read it as agricultural growth note that the parallel line speaks of the fruit of the land, that Isaiah does not use the word elsewhere as a title, and that the passage focuses on the remnant and the land rather than on a king. A middle view sees an intentional ambiguity: the land's renewal and the coming ruler belong together in the prophets' hope. The chapter's main point stands on any reading: after judgment God will give his people beauty, holiness, and his presence.

questions: The women of verse 1 are desperate for the security of a name. Where do people look for security and belonging when life collapses?
The survivors are called holy because God washes them. How does it change your idea of holiness to see it as something God gives rather than something we achieve?
The chapter pictures God's presence as shade from heat and shelter from storm. When have you needed God as that kind of refuge?
